relation: Separated from right ventricle by the interventricular septum
Connected to left atrium via the mitral valve
Ejects oxygenated blood into ascending aorta through the aortic valve
Surrounded circumferentially by myocardium (thickest in basal segments)
Forms the apex of the heart
morphology: Thick-walled, conical muscular chamber
Main systemic pumping chamber
Endocardial surface smooth except for papillary muscles
In echocardiography: appears as a circular structure in short-axis view, elliptical in long-axis

relation: Separated from left ventricle by the interventricular septum
Connected to right atrium via the tricuspid valve
Ejects deoxygenated blood into pulmonary artery through the pulmonary valve
Wrapped around the anterior and lateral aspects of the left ventricle
Shares the apex with the left ventricle
morphology: Thin-walled, crescent-shaped chamber in cross-section
Moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a characteristic internal structure
Wall thickness typically <5 mm in adults
Appears triangular in apical 4-chamber view

relation: Receives oxygenated blood from four pulmonary veins (not explicitly segmented here)
Connected to left ventricle via the mitral valve
Posterior wall adjacent to descending aorta and esophagus
Anterior wall adjacent to ascending aorta
morphology: Smooth-walled posterior chamber
Largest cardiac chamber by volume but often appears smaller in 2D imaging due to foreshortening
Left atrial appendage (not segmented) is a common site for thrombus in AF

relation: Receives systemic venous return via superior/inferior vena cava and coronary sinus
Connected to right ventricle via the tricuspid valve
Interatrial septum separates it from left atrium (fossa ovalis region)
morphology: Thin-walled chamber with prominent pectinate muscles in the appendage
Crista terminalis is an internal ridge separating smooth and trabeculated regions
Appears anterior and to the right of left atrium in standard views

relation: Comprises the muscular walls of both ventricles and parts of atria
Encases the left and right ventricular cavities
Contains the interventricular septum and left ventricular posterior wall as integral components
Surrounded externally by the pericardium
morphology: Striated cardiac muscle tissue with high echogenicity in ultrasound
Thickest around the left ventricle (8–12 mm in diastole), thinner around right ventricle (2–5 mm)
Contracts synchronously during systole to eject blood
Hypertrophy or thinning indicates pathological states (e.g., hypertension, infarction)

relation: Forms the medial boundary of both left and right ventricles
Composed of muscular (apical) and membranous (basal) portions
Adjacent to the aortic and mitral valves at its base
morphology: Curved muscular wall, thicker at base (~10–15 mm), thinner at apex
Moves toward the posterior wall during systole (normal contraction pattern)
In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, may show asymmetric thickening

relation: Separates the left atrium from the right atrium
Contains the fossa ovalis, a remnant of the fetal foramen ovale
Located posterior to the aortic root and anterior to the esophagus in axial orientation
Forms part of the medial wall of both atria
morphology: Thin, smooth muscular membrane (typically 2–4 mm thick in adults)
Fossa ovalis appears as an oval depression on the right atrial side, surrounded by a raised limbus
In echocardiography: best visualized in subcostal or transesophageal views as a linear echo-bright structure between atria
Aneurysm, perforation (e.g., patent foramen ovale), or tumor infiltration may alter its contour or mobility

relation: Refers specifically to the inferolateral wall of the left ventricle
Opposite the interventricular septum
Externally adjacent to the pericardium and often the descending aorta
morphology: Muscular segment of the left ventricle
Thickness similar to septum in healthy hearts (symmetric hypertrophy if both thickened)
Key region for assessing regional wall motion abnormalities (e.g., in inferior MI)

relation: Bicuspid valve connecting left atrium and left ventricle
Anterior leaflet adjacent to aortic valve (fibrous continuity)
Supported by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial)
morphology: Two leaflets: larger anterior (septal) and smaller posterior (mural)
Opens widely during diastole to allow LV filling
Coaptation line visible in systole; prolapse or flail indicates pathology

relation: Tricuspid valve connecting right atrium and right ventricle
Located more apically than the mitral valve
Separated from the pulmonary valve by the right ventricular outflow tract
morphology: Three leaflets: anterior, posterior, and septal
Thinner and more mobile than mitral valve
Regurgitation common in volume overload (e.g., pulmonary hypertension)

relation: Semilunar valve between left ventricle and ascending aorta
Fibrous continuity with the anterior mitral leaflet
Located centrally at the cardiac base
morphology: Three cusps: left, right, and non-coronary
Opens during systole to eject blood; closes sharply at end-systole
Calcification or fusion leads to stenosis; dilation causes regurgitation

relation: Semilunar valve between right ventricle and pulmonary artery
Located anterior and superior to the aortic valve
Separated from tricuspid valve by the right ventricular outflow tract
morphology: Three thin, delicate cusps
Less commonly diseased than aortic valve
Often difficult to visualize fully in standard echocardiographic views

relation: Arises directly from the left ventricle via the aortic valve
Gives rise to coronary arteries (not segmented)
Continuous with the aortic arch and descending aorta
morphology: Tubular, anechoic lumen with bright intimal borders in ultrasound
Diameter typically 25–37 mm in adults
Dilation suggests aneurysm or connective tissue disorder (e.g., Marfan syndrome)

relation: Continuation of the aortic arch
Runs posterior to the left atrium in the thorax
Visible in parasternal long-axis and suprasternal views
morphology: Circular cross-section in transverse imaging
Wall may show atherosclerotic plaques in elderly patients
Used as an acoustic window in some echo views

relation: Arises from the right ventricular outflow tract via the pulmonary valve
Bifurcates into left and right pulmonary arteries near the aortic arch
Runs anterior to the descending aorta
morphology: Large vessel with thin walls and low-pressure flow
Diameter increases in pulmonary hypertension
Main trunk diameter normally <25 mm
Catch-all category for unclassified or low-confidence structures
May include artifacts, noise, or rare anatomical variants
